claim: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0) tetramers form square arrays in lens membranes through a yet unknown mechanism.
source: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0) tetramers form square arrays in lens membranes through a yet unknown mechanism, but lens membranes are enriched in sphingomyelin and cholesterol.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a known observation without supporting data in this manuscript.

claim: Lens membranes are enriched in sphingomyelin and cholesterol.
source: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0) tetramers form square arrays in lens membranes through a yet unknown mechanism, but lens membranes are enriched in sphingomyelin and cholesterol.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Electron crystallographic structures of AQP0 in sphingomyelin/cholesterol membranes were determined.
source: Here, we determined electron crystallographic structures of AQP0 in sphingomyelin/cholesterol membranes and performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to establish that the observed cholesterol positions represent those seen around an isolated AQP0 tetramer and that the AQP0 tetramer largely defines the location and orientation of most of its associated cholesterol molecules.
evidence: The manuscript describes the determination of EC structures as a primary experimental result.

claim: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations establish that the observed cholesterol positions represent those seen around an isolated AQP0 tetramer.
source: Here, we determined electron crystallographic structures of AQP0 in sphingomyelin/cholesterol membranes and performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to establish that the observed cholesterol positions represent those seen around an isolated AQP0 tetramer and that the AQP0 tetramer largely defines the location and orientation of most of its associated cholesterol molecules.
evidence: MD simulations were performed and the results are described in the manuscript.

claim: The AQP0 tetramer largely defines the location and orientation of most of its associated cholesterol molecules.
source: Here, we determined electron crystallographic structures of AQP0 in sphingomyelin/cholesterol membranes and performed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to establish that the observed cholesterol positions represent those seen around an isolated AQP0 tetramer and that the AQP0 tetramer largely defines the location and orientation of most of its associated cholesterol molecules.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the MD simulation results presented in the manuscript.

claim: At a high concentration, cholesterol increases the hydrophobic thickness of the annular lipid shell around AQP0 tetramers.
source: At a high concentration, cholesterol increases the hydrophobic thickness of the annular lipid shell around AQP0 tetramers, which may thus cluster to mitigate the resulting hydrophobic mismatch.
evidence: This is based on measurements from the EC structures presented in the manuscript.

claim: AQP0 tetramers may cluster to mitigate the hydrophobic mismatch resulting from increased cholesterol concentration.
source: At a high concentration, cholesterol increases the hydrophobic thickness of the annular lipid shell around AQP0 tetramers, which may thus cluster to mitigate the resulting hydrophobic mismatch.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the observed structural changes.

claim: Neighboring AQP0 tetramers sandwich a cholesterol deep in the center of the membrane.
source: Moreover, neighboring AQP0 tetramers sandwich a cholesterol deep in the center of the membrane.
evidence: This is observed in the EC structure of AQP01SM:2Chol.

claim: The association of two AQP0 tetramers is necessary to maintain the deep cholesterol in its position.
source: MD simulations show that the association of two AQP0 tetramers is necessary to maintain the deep cholesterol in its position and that the deep cholesterol increases the force required to laterally detach two AQP0 tetramers, not only due to protein–protein contacts but also due to increased lipid–protein complementarity.
evidence: This is demonstrated through MD simulations presented in the manuscript.

claim: The deep cholesterol increases the force required to laterally detach two AQP0 tetramers.
source: MD simulations show that the association of two AQP0 tetramers is necessary to maintain the deep cholesterol in its position and that the deep cholesterol increases the force required to laterally detach two AQP0 tetramers, not only due to protein–protein contacts but also due to increased lipid–protein complementarity.
evidence: This is shown through force-probe MD simulations in the manuscript.

claim: The increased force required to detach AQP0 tetramers is due to both protein–protein contacts and increased lipid–protein complementarity.
source: MD simulations show that the association of two AQP0 tetramers is necessary to maintain the deep cholesterol in its position and that the deep cholesterol increases the force required to laterally detach two AQP0 tetramers, not only due to protein–protein contacts but also due to increased lipid–protein complementarity.
evidence: This is analyzed and demonstrated through MD simulations in the manuscript.

claim: Each AQP0 tetramer interacts with four 'glue' cholesterols.
source: Since each tetramer interacts with four such 'glue' cholesterols, avidity effects may stabilize larger arrays.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural arrangement observed in the EC structures.

claim: Avidity effects may stabilize larger AQP0 arrays.
source: Since each tetramer interacts with four such 'glue' cholesterols, avidity effects may stabilize larger arrays.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the structural observations.

claim: The principles proposed to drive AQP0 array formation could also underlie protein clustering in lipid rafts.
source: The principles proposed to drive AQP0 array formation could also underlie protein clustering in lipid rafts.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to a broader biological context.

claim: Proteins in biological membranes are densely packed and often organized into functional modules.
source: The current view of biological membranes is that proteins are densely packed and often organized into functional modules that perform specific biological functions (Engelman, 2005; Nicolson, 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Lipids play an important role in organizing membrane proteins.
source: Lipids play an important role in organizing membrane proteins, and the resulting specialized membrane domains are now commonly known as lipid microdomains or lipid rafts (Karnovsky et al., 1982; Lingwood and Simons, 2010; Simons and Ikonen, 1997; Simons and Toomre, 2000; Stier and Sackmann, 1973; Vereb et al., 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Lipid microdomains are enriched in cholesterol.
source: Lipid microdomains are enriched in cholesterol (Barenholz, 2002; Korade and Kenworthy, 2008; Simons and Ikonen, 1997) and characterized by a lipid phase that is distinct from the surrounding membrane (Ahmed et al., 1997; Schroeder et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Lipid microdomains are characterized by a lipid phase that is distinct from the surrounding membrane.
source: Lipid microdomains are enriched in cholesterol (Barenholz, 2002; Korade and Kenworthy, 2008; Simons and Ikonen, 1997) and characterized by a lipid phase that is distinct from the surrounding membrane (Ahmed et al., 1997; Schroeder et al., 1991).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol has a planar four-aromatic ring structure with a short isooctyl alkyl chain and a small 3-β-hydroxyl head group.
source: Cholesterol has a planar four-aromatic ring structure with a short isooctyl alkyl chain and a small 3-β-hydroxyl head group that can form a hydrogen bond with a polar group (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of cholesterol structure, which is established knowledge and also shown in a figure.

claim: Cholesterol features a smooth (or α) face and a rough (or β) face.
source: Because the aliphatic groups linked to the ring system are asymmetrically distributed, cholesterol features a smooth (or α) face and a rough (or β) face (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a description of cholesterol structure, which is established knowledge and also shown in a figure.

claim: Cholesterol makes up 40–90% of the lipids in eukaryotic cell membranes.
source: It makes up 40–90% of the lipids in eukaryotic cell membranes (Liscum and Munn, 1999; van Meer et al., 2008).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol can form non-covalent interactions with lipid acyl chains, preferentially with saturated ones.
source: Cholesterol can form non-covalent interactions with lipid acyl chains, preferentially with saturated ones (Epand and Epand, 2004; Zheng et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol can cause the membrane to transition from a liquid-disordered to a liquid-ordered phase.
source: As a result, the membrane can transition from a liquid-disordered to a liquid-ordered phase (de Meyer et al., 2010; Ghysels et al., 2019; Marsh, 2010; Seelig, 1977), which has been linked to the formation of lipid microdomains (Quinn and Wolf, 2009; Silvius, 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The liquid-ordered phase transition has been linked to the formation of lipid microdomains.
source: As a result, the membrane can transition from a liquid-disordered to a liquid-ordered phase (de Meyer et al., 2010; Ghysels et al., 2019; Marsh, 2010; Seelig, 1977), which has been linked to the formation of lipid microdomains (Quinn and Wolf, 2009; Silvius, 2003).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Mammalian lens membranes contain a high percentage of sphingomyelin and cholesterol.
source: Mammalian lens membranes contain a high percentage of sphingomyelin (SM) – a lipid consisting of a phosphocholine head group, a sphingosine amino alcohol, and a fatty acid (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) – and cholesterol, lipids that are characteristic for lipid rafts (Simons and Ikonen, 1997; Zelenka, 1984).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The human lens core plasma membrane features the highest molar cholesterol content of all membranes found in human tissues, with a molar ratio of cholesterol to other phospholipids ranging from 2.02 to 2.52.
source: With a molar ratio of cholesterol to other phospholipids ranging from 2.02 to 2.52, the human lens core plasma membrane features the highest molar cholesterol content of all membranes found in human tissues (Fleschner and Cenedella, 1991; Zelenka, 1984).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0) is a lens-specific water channel.
source: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0), a lens-specific water channel, is the most abundant membrane protein in lens membranes (over 60% of the total protein content) (Alcalá et al., 1975; Bloemendal et al., 1972), where it forms large two-dimensional (2D) arrays (Gorin et al., 1984; Kistler and Bullivant, 1980; Zampighi et al., 1982).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: AQP0 is the most abundant membrane protein in lens membranes (over 60% of the total protein content).
source: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0), a lens-specific water channel, is the most abundant membrane protein in lens membranes (over 60% of the total protein content) (Alcalá et al., 1975; Bloemendal et al., 1972), where it forms large two-dimensional (2D) arrays (Gorin et al., 1984; Kistler and Bullivant, 1980; Zampighi et al., 1982).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: AQP0 forms large two-dimensional (2D) arrays in lens membranes.
source: Aquaporin-0 (AQP0), a lens-specific water channel, is the most abundant membrane protein in lens membranes (over 60% of the total protein content) (Alcalá et al., 1975; Bloemendal et al., 1972), where it forms large two-dimensional (2D) arrays (Gorin et al., 1984; Kistler and Bullivant, 1980; Zampighi et al., 1982).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The structure of AQP0 was determined by electron crystallography of in vitro assembled 2D crystals grown with the lipid dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC).
source: The propensity of AQP0 to form 2D crystals was used to determine its structure by electron crystallography (EC) of in vitro assembled 2D crystals grown with the lipid dimyristoyl phosphatidylcholine (DMPC) (Gonen et al., 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: AQP0 2D crystals were grown with a variety of different lipids.
source: Later, AQP0 2D crystals were grown with a variety of different lipids (Hite et al., 2015; Hite et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: All AQP0 2D crystals had the same lattice constants, which were identical to those of AQP0 arrays in native lens membranes.
source: All these crystals had the same lattice constants, which were identical to those of AQP0 arrays in native lens membranes (Buzhynskyy et al., 2007).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: In vitro grown 2D crystals recapitulate the organization of AQP0 tetramers in 2D arrays in the native lens membrane.
source: Thus, in vitro grown 2D crystals recapitulate the organization of AQP0 tetramers in 2D arrays in the native lens membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that lattice constants are identical.

claim: High-resolution EC studies showed that AQP0 tetramers in the 2D crystals are separated by a layer of lipids and form essentially no direct protein–protein interactions.
source: Interestingly, however, high-resolution EC studies, which also resolved the annular lipids (Gonen et al., 2005; Hite et al., 2010), showed that AQP0 tetramers in the 2D crystals are separated by a layer of lipids and form essentially no direct protein–protein interactions.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: The crystal contacts in AQP0 2D crystals are almost exclusively mediated by lipids.
source: As the crystal contacts are almost exclusively mediated by lipids, it is surprising that AQP0 2D crystals could be obtained with almost every lipid tested.
evidence: This is an observation from previous EC studies.

claim: Initial MD simulations predicted the existence of a cholesterol hotspot at the extracellular side of the AQP0 surface.
source: Initial simulations probing the interactions of AQP0 with lipids were carried out with pure DMPC and mixed DMPC:cholesterol membrane patches, predicting the existence of a cholesterol hotspot at the extracellular side of the AQP0 surface (O'Connor and Klauda, 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: MD simulations demonstrated that the positions of lipids around AQP0 seen in EC structures are representative of the localization of unconstrained lipids around individual AQP0 tetramers.
source: Later, MD simulations demonstrated that the positions of lipids around AQP0 seen in EC structures obtained from 2D crystals, in which the lipids are constrained by the protein crystal packing, are indeed representative of the localization of unconstrained lipids around individual AQP0 tetramers (Aponte-Santamaría et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Protein mobility and surface roughness play key roles in defining lipid positions around AQP0.
source: Molecular aspects, such as protein mobility and surface roughness, were identified to play key roles in defining the lipid positions (Aponte-Santamaría et al., 2012; Briones et al., 2017).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Annular lipids adopt similar positions around several members of the aquaporin family.
source: Furthermore, a combination of coarse-grained and atomistic MD simulations revealed that annular lipids adopt similar positions around several members of the aquaporin family (Stansfeld et al., 2013), while mass spectrometry demonstrated the weak nature of the interaction of lipids with AQPZ (Laganowsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Mass spectrometry demonstrated the weak nature of the interaction of lipids with AQPZ.
source: Furthermore, a combination of coarse-grained and atomistic MD simulations revealed that annular lipids adopt similar positions around several members of the aquaporin family (Stansfeld et al., 2013), while mass spectrometry demonstrated the weak nature of the interaction of lipids with AQPZ (Laganowsky et al., 2014).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: AQP0 can be induced to form 2D crystals in vitro by choosing a very specific lipid-to-protein ratio (LPR) for reconstitution.
source: In vitro, AQP0 can be induced to form 2D crystals by choosing a very specific lipid-to-protein ratio (LPR) for reconstitution, but this in vitro approach does not explain why AQP0 tetramers form 2D arrays in native lens membranes, which contain an excess of lipids as well as other membrane proteins.
evidence: This is stated as an observation from previous work.

claim: Lipids mediate the interactions in AQP0 2D arrays.
source: Since lipids mediate the interactions in AQP0 2D arrays, it is likely that specific lipids play a role in the assembly of AQP0 2D arrays in the native lens membrane.
evidence: This is an inference based on previous structural observations.

claim: AQP0-containing lens membrane junctions are greatly enriched in cholesterol and sphingomyelin.
source: As AQP0-containing lens membrane junctions are greatly enriched in cholesterol and sphingomyelin (Fleschner and Cenedella, 1991), lipids that play a key role in raft formation (Brown and London, 2000), these lipids were prime candidates to drive AQP0 array formation.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol and sphingomyelin play a key role in raft formation.
source: As AQP0-containing lens membrane junctions are greatly enriched in cholesterol and sphingomyelin (Fleschner and Cenedella, 1991), lipids that play a key role in raft formation (Brown and London, 2000), these lipids were prime candidates to drive AQP0 array formation.
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: Purified AQP0 was reconstituted with mixtures of sphingomyelin and cholesterol at molar ratios of 1:0, 3:1, 2:1, 1:1, 1:2, 1:4, and 0:1.
source: Purified AQP0 was reconstituted with mixtures of sphingomyelin and cholesterol at molar ratios of 1:0, 3:1, 2:1, 1:1, 1:2, 1:4, and 0:1 (Figure 1A–E).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental procedure performed in this study.

claim: Every lipid mixture yielded membranes.
source: Every lipid mixture yielded membranes, which had a sheet-like morphology at sphingomyelin:cholesterol ratios of up to 1:2 and formed vesicles at higher cholesterol percentages.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Membranes had a sheet-like morphology at sphingomyelin:cholesterol ratios of up to 1:2.
source: Every lipid mixture yielded membranes, which had a sheet-like morphology at sphingomyelin:cholesterol ratios of up to 1:2 and formed vesicles at higher cholesterol percentages.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Membranes formed vesicles at higher cholesterol percentages.
source: Every lipid mixture yielded membranes, which had a sheet-like morphology at sphingomyelin:cholesterol ratios of up to 1:2 and formed vesicles at higher cholesterol percentages.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Power spectra of images taken of trehalose-embedded samples showed diffraction spots consistent with typical 2D arrays of AQP0 for every lipid mixture.
source: In every case, power spectra of images taken of trehalose-embedded samples showed diffraction spots consistent with typical 2D arrays of AQP0 (data not shown).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Cholesterol on its own does not form bilayers under physiological conditions and requires a molecule of complementary shape to do so.
source: Cholesterol on its own does not form bilayers under physiological conditions and requires a molecule of complementary shape to do so (Kumar, 1991; Raguz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature.

claim: AQP0 appears to fulfill the requirement for cholesterol to form membranes.
source: AQP0 appears to fulfill this requirement as it does form membranes with cholesterol.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that AQP0 forms membranes with pure cholesterol.

claim: Reconstitution of AQP0 with cholesterol only yielded membranes within a narrow LPR range, from 0.2 to 0.4.
source: However, reconstitution of AQP0 with cholesterol only yielded membranes within a narrow LPR range, from 0.2 to 0.4.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: At higher or lower LPRs than 0.2 to 0.4, only protein aggregates and no membranes were observed for AQP0 with cholesterol.
source: At higher or lower LPRs, only protein aggregates and no membranes were observed.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: AQP0 2D crystals formed with cholesterol at an LPR of 0.4 have the same lattice constants as all other AQP0 2D crystals analyzed to date (a=65.5 Å, b=65.5 Å, and γ=90°).
source: Fourier transforms of cryo-EM images of trehalose-embedded AQP0 2D crystals formed with cholesterol at an LPR of 0.4 showed clear reflections (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), establishing that the crystals have the same lattice constants as all other AQP0 2D crystals analyzed to date (a=65.5 Å, b=65.5 Å, and γ=90°).
evidence: This is based on analysis of cryo-EM images in this study.

claim: AQP0 crystals formed with cholesterol have p422 plane symmetry.
source: Phase comparisons of the reflections showed that the crystals have p422 plane symmetry (Table 1) and thus have to be double-layered.
evidence: This is based on analysis of diffraction data in this study.

claim: AQP0 crystals formed with cholesterol have to be double-layered.
source: Phase comparisons of the reflections showed that the crystals have p422 plane symmetry (Table 1) and thus have to be double-layered.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed symmetry.

claim: Merging of 15 images yielded a projection map at 3.2 Å resolution for AQP0 in pure cholesterol.
source: Merging of 15 images yielded a projection map at 3.2 Å resolution (Figure 1F and Table 2).
evidence: This is a result from the data processing in this study.

claim: AQP0 tetramers in a pure cholesterol membrane are organized in the same way as in membranes formed with all other lipids analyzed to date.
source: Although the crystals were not of sufficient quality to determine a high-resolution three-dimensional (3D) density map, the 2D projection map shows that AQP0 tetramers in a pure cholesterol membrane are organized in the same way as in membranes formed with all other lipids analyzed to date.
evidence: This is an inference based on the 2D projection map.

claim: Electron diffraction patterns of AQP0 crystals obtained with sphingomyelin/cholesterol mixtures showed reflections to a resolution of about 2 Å.
source: Fourier transforms of images of trehalose-embedded AQP0 crystals obtained with sphingomyelin/cholesterol mixtures showed reflections to a resolution of about 2 Å (Chiu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from previous work by the same authors.

claim: Diffraction patterns recorded from untilted AQP02SM:1Chol crystals showed reflections to a resolution of 2 Å.
source: While diffraction patterns recorded from untilted crystals showed reflections to a resolution of 2 Å (Figure 2A), reflections in diffraction patterns from highly tilted crystals were not visible beyond a resolution of 2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Reflections in diffraction patterns from highly tilted AQP02SM:1Chol crystals were not visible beyond a resolution of 2.5 Å.
source: While diffraction patterns recorded from untilted crystals showed reflections to a resolution of 2 Å (Figure 2A), reflections in diffraction patterns from highly tilted crystals were not visible beyond a resolution of 2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: A 3D density map at 2.5 Å resolution was calculated for AQP02SM:1Chol after merging 214 diffraction patterns from crystals tilted up to ~72°.
source: After merging 214 diffraction patterns from crystals tilted up to ~72° and phasing the intensity dataset by molecular replacement, we were able to calculate a 3D density map at 2.5 Å resolution (Figure 2B), which made it possible to model the AQP0 structure.
evidence: This is a result from the data processing in this study.

claim: The final model for AQP02SM:1Chol includes seven sphingomyelin molecules, SM1–SM7, with acyl chains ranging from 11 to 16 carbon atoms in length.
source: The final model includes seven sphingomyelin molecules, SM1–SM7, with acyl chains ranging from 11 to 16 carbon atoms in length (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the model building in this study.

claim: One density in the AQP02SM:1Chol map was consistent with the characteristic four-ring structure of cholesterol and was modeled as Chol1.
source: The one density in the map that was consistent with the characteristic four-ring structure of cholesterol was modeled as Chol1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a result from the model building in this study.

claim: The density in the center of four adjacent AQP0 tetramers around the fourfold symmetry axis in AQP02SM:1Chol was poorly resolved and could not be modeled.
source: The density in the center of four adjacent AQP0 tetramers around the fourfold symmetry axis was poorly resolved and could not be modeled (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the model building in this study.

claim: AQP0 in the 2:1 sphingomyelin/cholesterol membrane adopts the same conformation as it does in a DMPC bilayer, with RMSD between the Cα atoms of 0.271 Å.
source: AQP0 in the 2:1 sphingomyelin/cholesterol membrane adopts the same conformation as it does in a DMPC bilayer, AQP0DMPC (Gonen et al., 2005), and in an E. coli polar lipid extract (EPL) bilayer, AQP0EPL (Hite et al., 2010), with root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the Cα atoms of 0.271 Å and 0.264 Å, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison in this study.

claim: AQP0 in the 2:1 sphingomyelin/cholesterol membrane adopts the same conformation as it does in an E. coli polar lipid extract (EPL) bilayer, with RMSD between the Cα atoms of 0.264 Å.
source: AQP0 in the 2:1 sphingomyelin/cholesterol membrane adopts the same conformation as it does in a DMPC bilayer, AQP0DMPC (Gonen et al., 2005), and in an E. coli polar lipid extract (EPL) bilayer, AQP0EPL (Hite et al., 2010), with root mean square deviation (RMSD) between the Cα atoms of 0.271 Å and 0.264 Å, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison in this study.

claim: The water pathway through the AQP0 subunits in AQP02SM:1Chol showed density for four water molecules, at positions similar to those seen in previous EC AQP0 structures.
source: The water pathway through the AQP0 subunits showed density for four water molecules, at positions similar to those seen in previous EC AQP0 structures (Gonen et al., 2004; Hite et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study, compared to previous structures.

claim: The seven sphingomyelin molecules in AQP02SM:1Chol assume similar positions as the DMPC and EPL lipids in previous structures.
source: Comparison of the lipid bilayer in the AQP02SM:1Chol structure (Figure 3A) with those in the AQP0DMPC and AQP0EPL structures (Figure 3B and C) shows that the seven sphingomyelin molecules assume similar positions as the DMPC and EPL lipids, further strengthening the earlier conclusion that annular lipids are not randomly distributed around a membrane protein but assume preferred positions (Hite et al., 2010).
evidence: This is based on structural comparison in this study.

claim: The density for sphingomyelin SM3 in AQP02SM:1Chol is well defined.
source: The density for sphingomyelin SM3 is well defined.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: The carbonyl oxygen of the SM3 head group is hydrogen-bonded with the tyrosyl side chain of Tyr105 and the amide oxygen of the guanidinium side chain of Arg196.
source: The carbonyl oxygen of its head group is hydrogen-bonded with the tyrosyl side chain of Tyr105 and the amide oxygen of the guanidinium side chain of Arg196 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: The head groups of the remaining sphingomyelin lipids in AQP02SM:1Chol do not form specific interactions with AQP0.
source: However, the head groups of the remaining sphingomyelin lipids do not form specific interactions with AQP0, as reported for the DMPC and EPL head groups in the previous AQP0DMPC and AQP0EPL structures.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study, compared to previous structures.

claim: The sphingomyelin acyl chains in AQP02SM:1Chol follow grooves on the surface of AQP0.
source: Also, as observed in those structures, the sphingomyelin acyl chains follow grooves on the surface of AQP0.
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study, compared to previous structures.

claim: Chol1 in AQP02SM:1Chol is located in the extracellular leaflet.
source: The only cholesterol molecule, Chol1, resolved in the AQP02SM:1Chol structure is located in the extracellular leaflet (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: The tetracyclic ring of Chol1 makes π-stacking interactions with AQP0 residues His201 and Trp205.
source: The tetracyclic ring of Chol1 makes π-stacking interactions with AQP0 residues His201 and Trp205, and its alkyl tail makes van der Waals interactions with residues Ile87 and Val90 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: The alkyl tail of Chol1 makes van der Waals interactions with residues Ile87 and Val90.
source: The tetracyclic ring of Chol1 makes π-stacking interactions with AQP0 residues His201 and Trp205, and its alkyl tail makes van der Waals interactions with residues Ile87 and Val90 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: Chol1 interacts extensively with the adjacent sphingolipid in the extracellular leaflet, SM2.
source: Chol1 also interacts extensively with the adjacent sphingolipid in the extracellular leaflet, SM2, the acyl chains of which assume an all anti-dihedral conformation, increasing their conformational order (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: The acyl chains of SM2 assume an all anti-dihedral conformation, increasing their conformational order.
source: Chol1 also interacts extensively with the adjacent sphingolipid in the extracellular leaflet, SM2, the acyl chains of which assume an all anti-dihedral conformation, increasing their conformational order (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is an observation from the structure in this study.

claim: AQP0 2D crystals grown at a molar sphingomyelin:cholesterol ratio of 1:2 were better ordered than those at 2:1.
source: These crystals were even better ordered, and electron diffraction patterns of untilted specimens showed reflections to a resolution better than 1.6 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Electron diffraction patterns of untilted AQP01SM:2Chol specimens showed reflections to a resolution better than 1.6 Å.
source: These crystals were even better ordered, and electron diffraction patterns of untilted specimens showed reflections to a resolution better than 1.6 Å (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: Diffraction patterns of AQP01SM:2Chol 2D crystals tilted to 60° showed reflections to a resolution of ~2.5 Å.
source: Diffraction patterns of 2D crystals tilted to 60° showed reflections to a resolution of ~2.5 Å (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments performed in this study.

claim: A density map for AQP01SM:2Chol at 2.5 Å resolution was obtained.
source: We used the same data collection and processing scheme for AQP02SM:1Chol to obtain a density map for AQP01SM:2Chol at 2.5 Å resolution (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a result from the data processing in this study.

claim: The AQP01SM:2Chol density map allowed modeling of AQP0, five sphingomyelin molecules (SM2, SM3, SM5, SM6, and SM7), as well as four cholesterols.
source: The density map allowed us to model AQP0, five sphingomyelin molecules, SM2, SM3, SM5, SM6, and SM7 (numbers corresponding to the sphingomyelin molecules in AQP02SM:1Chol), as well as four cholesterols (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the model building in this study.

claim: It was not possible to model lipids in the area near the fourfold axis in AQP01SM:2Chol, where four AQP0 tetramers come together.
